paragraphs: The paper studies how to allocate measurements when testing many candidates against a common baseline. Each candidate has an unknown mean, and candidates above the baseline count as true positives. Because each candidate can be measured repeatedly, the experimenter can choose where to collect more evidence as results arrive.

The proposed algorithm uses ideas from multi-armed bandits to make those sampling decisions adaptively. Its objective is to discover a target proportion of the true positives using as few measurements as possible, while maintaining control over false discoveries throughout the process. This anytime requirement makes error control part of the ongoing experiment, rather than something assessed only at a predetermined endpoint.

The authors provide sample complexity results that match known information-theoretic lower bounds. Simulations also show substantial improvements over uniform sampling and an adaptive elimination approach. Together, these findings support the value of directing measurements toward useful candidates while retaining statistical safeguards. The abstract identifies biological research, drug discovery, and testing multiple online alternatives as promising applications, rather than reporting deployments in those settings.
neurips-2018-a-bandit-approach-to-sequen.tldr: An adaptive bandit-based testing method seeks sample-efficient discovery while controlling false discoveries throughout the experiment.

paragraphs: A GAN trains a generator against a discriminator that tries to distinguish generated samples from real data. With an unrestricted discriminator, this competition can be interpreted as minimizing a divergence between distributions. The paper asks how that interpretation changes when the discriminator can represent only a restricted collection of functions, as happens in practice.

The authors develop a convex duality framework to answer this question. For a convex discriminator class, the original GAN objective becomes a search for a generator close in Jensen-Shannon divergence to distributions that are penalized for failing to match data moments. The discriminator class determines which moments matter. This connects the discriminator's expressive restrictions to the distributional properties the training objective encourages.

The interpretation also extends to f-GAN and Wasserstein GAN. The framework additionally yields a hybrid of f-divergence and Wasserstein distance that changes continuously with the generative model. That theoretical property motivates controlling the discriminator's Lipschitz constant in standard GAN and f-GAN training. The authors numerically evaluate these regularization schemes, linking their analysis to practical training behavior.
neurips-2018-a-convex-duality-framework-.tldr: A convex duality framework explains how restricted discriminators shape GAN objectives and motivates regularization for smoother training objectives.

paragraphs: When another agent changes its behavior during interaction, a previously effective response may stop working. This paper studies that problem in Markov games, focusing on how an agent can recognize its counterpart's current policy and reuse an appropriate response. The challenge combines identifying behavior with adapting quickly enough to benefit from that identification.

The proposed deep BPR+ algorithm extends Bayesian policy reuse with a neural network that approximates the value function. Its rectified belief model uses an opponent model to infer the other agent's policy from both observed behavior and reward signals. These two evidence sources inform the agent's beliefs about which policy it is facing.

The method also replaces separately stored policies with a distilled policy network serving as a policy library. This supports online learning and reuse within the same approach. In complex Markov games using raw visual inputs, the authors report better policy detection accuracy, cumulative reward, and convergence speed than existing algorithms. The findings support combining richer opponent inference with a compact reusable policy representation for the evaluated changing-agent settings.
neurips-2018-a-deep-bayesian-policy-reus.tldr: Deep BPR+ combines opponent inference and distilled policy reuse to improve adaptation to changing agents in evaluated Markov games.

paragraphs: A stochastic multi-armed bandit algorithm learns which actions to choose from the rewards it observes. This paper examines what happens when an attacker can manipulate those reward signals. The attack targets the feedback driving learning, allowing the attacker to influence later action choices through the evidence the algorithm receives.

The authors develop attacks against two widely used algorithms, epsilon-greedy and UCB, without requiring knowledge of the actions' mean rewards. That distinction matters because the attacker does not need the underlying reward averages in advance to steer behavior. The paper characterizes the required attack effort as logarithmic, multiplied by a problem-specific factor that decreases when the setting is easier to attack.

The result shows that these learning algorithms can be redirected to favor or suppress particular actions with limited manipulation effort under the studied setup. A medical treatment is given as an example of an action whose selection could be affected, rather than as a reported deployment. The contribution exposes a security weakness in relying on reward feedback that an adversary can alter.
neurips-2018-adversarial-attacks-on-stoc.tldr: Reward manipulation can steer epsilon-greedy and UCB bandits with logarithmic attack effort without knowing their mean rewards.

paragraphs: Small changes to an image can cause a computer vision model to assign an incorrect label. The paper investigates whether adversarial images can also affect human judgments. It focuses on observers with limited viewing time, making the conditions of human perception central to the question being tested.

The approach builds on techniques for transferring adversarial examples between computer vision models. Such techniques construct examples using a model with known architecture and parameters, then seek effects on models whose details are unknown. The authors combine this transfer-based approach with matching the initial processing of the human visual system, connecting the attack design to the human viewing setting.

The reported finding is that adversarial examples with strong transfer across computer vision models influence classifications by time-limited human observers. This establishes an effect under the studied viewing conditions; it does not establish the same result for unrestricted inspection. The contribution connects model-to-model adversarial transfer with human classification behavior, showing that these perturbations can matter beyond the computer vision systems used to construct them.
neurips-2018-adversarial-examples-that-f.tldr: Adversarial images that transfer strongly between vision models also influence human classifications when viewing time is limited.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether adversarial vulnerability reflects limits that extend beyond particular classifier designs. Its analysis assumes that a smooth generative model produces the data. Within this setting, the question is how robust a classification function can be against input perturbations, rather than how to improve one specific trained network.

The authors derive upper bounds on robustness that apply to any classification function under their assumptions. They also prove the existence of adversarial perturbations that transfer well between classifiers with small risk. This connects vulnerability across different classifiers to the shared data-generating setting, rather than treating every successful transfer as an isolated property of a particular model pair.

The analysis further relates robustness to properties of the generative model, including smoothness and the dimensionality of its latent space. Numerical experiments on several datasets indicate that the bounds provide informative reference points for the greatest achievable robustness. The scope of the conclusion rests on the smooth generative-model assumption: the contribution is a conditional account of fundamental limits, supported by numerical evidence.
neurips-2018-adversarial-vulnerability-f.tldr: Under a smooth generative-model assumption, the paper bounds classifier robustness and proves transferable adversarial perturbations exist.

paragraphs: Blending faces often makes the result appear more attractive, but this preference depends on context. Recognizing the original faces can weaken the effect, while categorizing race or gender before judging certain blends can reverse it. The paper seeks a statistical explanation for why averaging can produce different attractiveness judgments.

The authors hypothesize that people prefer objects requiring less encoding effort, particularly those perceived as statistically typical. A blend can appear attractive because it is more likely under the relevant face distribution. A preceding task can change which features enter the representation, however, changing what counts as typical within that restricted feature space. The same coding-cost principle can therefore account for both increased and decreased attractiveness.

Simulations provide a quantitative account of these opposing effects, and the authors validate the model with data from a gender categorization task. They also propose an experiment to distinguish their account from an explanation based on difficult categorization producing negative feelings. That experiment is a proposed test, while the presented evidence supports the statistical account as a model of contextual preference.
neurips-2018-beauty-in-averageness-and-i.tldr: A statistical coding-cost model explains how context can make blended faces seem either more or less attractive.

paragraphs: Metric learning builds a distance measure intended to reflect meaningful similarities between samples. The paper argues that extracting features before learning this distance can leave the two stages poorly matched. Features may also neglect local relationships among samples or noise in the data, reducing their usefulness for the recognition task.

The proposed model joins feature extraction and distance learning in a bilevel optimization problem. At the lower level, graph-regularized sparse coefficients represent the data's underlying structure. At the upper level, the learned distance brings samples from the same class closer and separates samples from different classes. This ties the representation of each sample to the classification relationships the distance should express.

To solve the coupled problem, the authors use Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions and an alternating direction method to derive an efficient algorithm. Experiments on multiple datasets containing occluded images demonstrate effectiveness and robustness in those settings. The contribution is the joint treatment of representation and distance: structural information used to describe the data becomes part of learning how recognition should compare samples.
neurips-2018-bilevel-distance-metric-lea.tldr: A bilevel optimization model jointly learns structured features and discriminative distances, showing robustness on occluded-image datasets.

paragraphs: Understanding an indoor image in three dimensions requires estimating objects, room layout, and the camera's pose together. These predictions must describe a compatible scene. The paper introduces an end-to-end model that estimates all three from a single RGB image in real time, treating their relationships as part of the prediction problem.

The model represents three-dimensional object boxes through predictions from modules for camera pose and object attributes. This parameterization helps preserve agreement between the image and the reconstructed world, reducing variation in predicted three-dimensional coordinates. It also creates a way to impose shared constraints across modules, so training can account for their combined geometric consequences.

Three cooperative losses address object boxes, their two-dimensional projections, and physical constraints. They support joint training and inference toward geometrically consistent, physically plausible scenes. On SUN RGB-D, the authors report significant improvements over prior approaches in layout estimation, object detection, camera pose estimation, and overall scene understanding. These results support coordinating the component predictions through shared structure rather than evaluating each component's training objective in isolation.
neurips-2018-cooperative-holistic-scene-.tldr: A jointly trained model uses shared geometric and physical constraints to recover indoor objects, room layout, and camera pose from one image.

paragraphs: Multitask reinforcement learning faces a scaling problem as the number of tasks or collected trajectories increases. The paper identifies reliance on centralized solutions as a main source of this difficulty. Distributing the computation is therefore part of making the learning problem manageable, rather than simply a change in where the same calculations run.

Earlier approaches used connections between multitask reinforcement learning and consensus problems to develop scalable methods. According to the abstract, those approaches relied on predefined objectives and offered linear convergence guarantees. The authors instead derive the multitask learning formulation from a variational inference perspective, providing a different basis for constructing the optimization problem.

They then introduce a distributed solver with quadratic convergence guarantees. The claimed advance concerns both the formulation of multitask learning and the convergence behavior of its solver. Quadratic convergence describes how optimization error decreases during convergence; it is not itself a fixed wall-clock speedup. The paper's stated contribution is a distributed inference-based approach with a stronger convergence guarantee than the linear guarantees described for earlier methods.
neurips-2018-distributed-multitask-reinf.tldr: The paper derives multitask reinforcement learning through variational inference and introduces a distributed solver with quadratic convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper incorporates fairness directly into the problem used to train a classifier. Its chosen requirement encourages conditional risk to remain approximately constant as a sensitive variable changes. This makes fairness a constraint on the classifier's error behavior across sensitive-variable values, alongside the usual objective of reducing prediction loss.

The authors derive bounds for both prediction risk and fairness that support statistical consistency of the method. Addressing both quantities matters because a useful constrained learner must account for predictive performance as well as the fairness condition it was designed to satisfy. The theoretical results connect learning from finite data to these two objectives.

For kernel methods, the fairness requirement produces an orthogonality constraint that can be incorporated into training. For linear models, it becomes a simple preprocessing operation on the data. These specializations make the general formulation concrete for established learning methods. Experiments indicate favorable performance against existing approaches. The findings concern the paper's specific conditional-risk fairness criterion, providing a statistically supported and empirically evaluated way to impose it.
neurips-2018-empirical-risk-minimization.tldr: A fairness-constrained learning approach encourages similar conditional risk across sensitive-variable values, with theoretical bounds and practical kernel and linear formulations.

paragraphs: The paper presents a physics simulator that can function as a differentiable component inside a neural network. This allows a larger learning system to include structured physical knowledge while adjusting its parameters from data. Simulation becomes part of the trainable computation, connecting observed behavior to the physical model used to reproduce it.

The technical contribution is analytical backpropagation through a simulator formulated as a linear complementarity problem. Instead of estimating gradients with finite differences, the method computes them analytically through the simulation. These gradients allow information about a mismatch between predictions and observations to guide changes in the surrounding learning system.

Experiments across diverse domains demonstrate learning physical parameters, matching and simulating observed visual behavior, and enabling control through gradient-based planning. The abstract also highlights sample efficiency from embedding physical structure in the system. These findings show how the same differentiable engine can support both explaining observations and selecting actions. The authors include code for the engine and experiments, making the proposed simulation component available alongside the work.
neurips-2018-end-to-end-differentiable-p.tldr: An analytically differentiable physics engine enables end-to-end learning of physical behavior and gradient-based control.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can struggle with sparse rewards, ineffective exploration, and sensitivity to hyperparameters. Evolutionary methods offer population-based exploration and evaluate policies through fitness, but often require many samples and have difficulty optimizing numerous parameters. The paper combines these approaches to use their complementary strengths in continuous control.

Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning maintains an evolutionary population whose experiences provide diverse training data for a reinforcement learning agent. Periodically, that agent is inserted back into the population. This creates a two-way exchange: evolutionary search supplies experience, while the gradient-trained agent brings improvements obtained through reinforcement learning into the evolutionary process.

The method combines fitness-based temporal credit assignment and policy diversity with off-policy learning's ability to reuse data and exploit gradients. The population also provides the stability associated with a population-based approach. Experiments across challenging continuous-control benchmarks report significant improvements over prior reinforcement learning and evolutionary methods. The results support this reciprocal interaction as a useful way to combine exploration with more sample-efficient policy improvement in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2018-evolution-guided-policy-gra.tldr: Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning exchanges experience and policies between an evolutionary population and a gradient-trained agent to improve continuous control.

paragraphs: Quantizing recurrent neural networks can reduce storage, memory use, and computation for resource-limited devices. Extremely low precision, however, can cause large accuracy losses. The authors examine different quantization schemes and the distributions of full-precision tensor values to understand why the same treatment may not suit every part of a recurrent model.

Their observations motivate HitNet, which uses different quantization methods for weights and activations because these quantities have different distributions. The method represents values using only minus one, zero, and one. It also introduces a sloping factor into activation functions, motivated by earlier work on Boltzmann machines, to further narrow the accuracy gap.

Results on LSTM and GRU models improve substantially over earlier quantization methods. On Penn Tree Bank, ternary LSTM perplexity decreases from 126 to 110.3, compared with 97.2 for full precision. Ternary GRU perplexity decreases from 142 to 113.5, compared with 102.7 for full precision. These examples show a meaningful reduction in the quantization penalty while retaining a measurable gap from the full-precision models.
neurips-2018-hitnet-hybrid-ternary-recur.tldr: HitNet uses hybrid ternary quantization for recurrent networks to substantially reduce accuracy losses relative to earlier low-precision methods.

paragraphs: In online linear regression, a learner predicts a number after seeing each input vector, then receives the label and incurs squared error. Performance is measured against the best fixed linear predictor chosen afterward. Earlier work could compute the minimax strategy backward from the game's end, but needed the entire input sequence in advance.

The authors show how to reverse that computation into a forward recursion when a measure of the problem's scale is supplied. The learner can then follow the minimax strategy without knowing future inputs. Optimality also holds against adaptively chosen inputs and labels, provided the adversary obeys constraints that prevent it from misrepresenting the supplied scale.

The resulting strategy and regret depend on the constraint set's size rather than the number of rounds. Consequently, the strategy incurs no more regret than the optimum that knows the horizon beforehand. The paper also interprets the algorithm as follow-the-regularized-leader with a data-dependent regularizer and gives an explicit minimax regret expression. The scale information and adversarial constraints are essential qualifications to the stated guarantee.
neurips-2018-horizon-independent-minimax.tldr: Given scale information and suitable adversarial constraints, online linear regression can achieve minimax performance without knowing future inputs or the horizon.

paragraphs: Studies of decision-making often fit a model to people's choices and then look for brain signals associated with the model's internal quantities. The paper identifies a weakness in this sequence: a model fitted only to behavior has internal mechanisms unconstrained by neural measurements. Those mechanisms may therefore miss or mischaracterize relevant brain activity.

The authors introduce recurrent neural network models fitted jointly to behavioral and fMRI data. Training encourages internal states to relate appropriately to neural activity while the network predicts the subject's next action. This makes both the observed choices and the recorded brain signals contribute to the learned account of decision-making.

The fitted model also supports a visualization linking activity in different brain regions after a reward to subsequent choices. Using a previously published dataset, the method recovers neural substrates identified through explicit model engineering in earlier work and produces additional findings about temporal activity patterns. The results support joint fitting as a way to connect flexible behavioral prediction with measured neural dynamics, including how those relationships unfold over time.
neurips-2018-integrated-accounts-of-beha.tldr: Jointly fitting recurrent networks to choices and fMRI signals connects behavioral prediction with the timing of measured brain activity.

paragraphs: Finite feature maps make nonlinear kernel methods more computationally manageable, but reducing the number of features can sacrifice approximation quality. This paper asks how to choose a small, useful set of explicit features from multiple kernels. Its method builds that set sequentially, selecting candidates greedily according to a correlation measure.

The authors establish a test-error bound separating two contributions. One reflects approximation using the selected explicit features; the other depends on spectral properties of the best model in the combined kernel's Hilbert space. This distinction explains why the usefulness of a compact feature representation depends on the structure of the underlying model as well as on feature selection.

When the best underlying model is sufficiently sparse that spectral error is negligible, the bound permits test-error control with a small feature set whose size can grow polylogarithmically with the data. This is a conditional result, not a guarantee for every dataset. Empirically, at a fixed feature count, the method can obtain lower test error with less computation time than leading data-dependent random-feature methods.
neurips-2018-learning-bounds-for-greedy-.tldr: Greedy feature selection across kernels offers compact approximations with test-error guarantees when the underlying model is sufficiently sparse.

paragraphs: Predicting team outcomes by adding individual player scores assumes that a player's contribution is independent of teammates. The paper addresses the missing interaction effects: some combinations perform unusually well together, while others perform poorly. It proposes models that learn from group comparisons while representing these dependencies between members.

Explicitly modeling player interactions creates a scaling challenge because the number of possible pairs grows quadratically with the player population. For large populations, the authors introduce a latent factor model to make the problem tractable. They also bound its sample complexity under mild assumptions, providing a theoretical account of the data needed for learning in that setting.

On several esports datasets, the proposed models have much stronger predictive performance than earlier approaches. They also reveal patterns that methods based only on individual effects cannot discover. These findings give interaction modeling two roles: improving predictions of group outcomes and exposing relationships among members. The results support treating a team's composition as more informative than the sum of independently estimated player strengths.
neurips-2018-learning-from-group-compari.tldr: Models of player interactions improve esports outcome predictions and use latent factors to address the growth in possible teammate relationships.

paragraphs: Training neural networks with very few examples can produce overfitting and catastrophic forgetting. Generating additional examples is one remedy, but useful augmentation must capture how examples within a class vary. The paper challenges approaches that either transfer within-class variation too broadly or generate a finite collection without modeling the underlying latent distribution.

The proposed Covariance-Preserving Adversarial Augmentation Network uses a GAN to model each new class's latent distribution with help from related base classes. Estimating that distribution directly from scarce new-class data can introduce bias. The method therefore explicitly preserves covariance information from base examples during generation, using it to represent patterns of variability.

The authors report that generated examples are both realistic and diverse, and that this leads to substantial improvements over the state of the art on ImageNet. The central idea is to make transferred variability an explicit part of generation. The empirical findings support using related base-class structure to improve augmentation when the new class itself supplies little evidence about its distribution.
neurips-2018-low-shot-learning-via-covar.tldr: A covariance-preserving GAN transfers variability from related base classes to generate useful examples for low-shot learning.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer a route toward low-power computation based on discrete spike events. Training deep versions is difficult because the function that generates a spike is not differentiable, preventing direct use of standard backpropagation. The paper introduces SLAYER as a learning mechanism that addresses this obstacle while accounting for the temporal nature of spikes.

The method learns both synaptic weights and axonal delays. Its temporal credit assignment policy sends error information back to preceding layers, connecting learning to when signals occur as well as to their strengths. This makes timing part of the training problem rather than treating the network solely as a collection of static weighted connections.

The authors release a GPU-accelerated implementation supporting fully connected and convolutional architectures. They compare the method with existing spiking-network learning approaches and techniques that convert conventional neural networks into spiking ones. Reported results reach state-of-the-art SNN performance on MNIST, NMNIST, DVS Gesture, and TIDIGITS. The findings support the proposed backpropagation mechanism as an effective training approach across the evaluated spiking-network tasks.
neurips-2018-slayer-spike-layer-error-re.tldr: SLAYER trains spiking networks through temporal error assignment, learning connection weights and delays while addressing non-differentiable spike generation.

paragraphs: Sparse regression seeks a model with relatively few nonzero coefficients. This paper analyzes orthogonal matching pursuit, a widely used greedy algorithm, with attention to both identifying the relevant variables and predicting beyond the observed data. Recovering the support means identifying which entries of the sparse vector are nonzero.

The analysis assumes that the objective satisfies restricted strong convexity. Under that condition, the authors obtain a support recovery result and a generalization error bound. These address related but distinct questions: whether the algorithm can locate the sparse model's active components, and how well its learned predictor can generalize.

The authors also derive lower bounds for orthogonal matching pursuit that match their upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. This indicates that the guarantees are close to the algorithm's limits in the analyzed setting, rather than merely being loose sufficient estimates. They describe these as the first such matching support recovery and generalization bounds for a sparse regression algorithm under restricted strong convexity, to the best of their knowledge.
neurips-2018-support-recovery-for-orthog.tldr: Under restricted strong convexity, orthogonal matching pursuit has support recovery and generalization bounds that match lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: The paper studies a two-layer neural network called the committee machine in a teacher-student setting. It examines both the best learning performance the available information permits and what an efficient algorithm can achieve. These are different questions because the existence of an accurate solution does not by itself supply an efficient way to find it.

The authors rigorously justify statistical-physics approaches previously used heuristically to calculate optimal learning and generalization errors for neural networks. They also introduce an approximate message passing algorithm for the committee machine. Across a large set of parameters, this algorithm achieves optimal learning in polynomial time, connecting the theoretical optimum with a computationally efficient procedure.

Other parameter regimes exhibit a gap: low generalization error is information-theoretically possible, but the proposed algorithm does not attain it. The authors interpret this as strong evidence for computational difficulty and suggest that no efficient algorithm exists in those regimes. That suggestion is stronger than the directly established algorithmic failure, so it remains evidence for a computational barrier rather than a universal impossibility proof.
neurips-2018-the-committee-machine-compu.tldr: Rigorous committee-machine analysis identifies regimes where optimal learning is efficient and others suggesting a gap between statistical possibility and computational feasibility.

paragraphs: Language changes across time, domains, and topics, and word embeddings offer a way to study those differences. This paper introduces the global anchor method for measuring shifts at the level of whole text collections. Its target is the relationship between corpora, including how language evolves and how domains differ.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that global anchors and the widely used embedding-alignment approach are equivalent in their ability to detect corpus-level shifts. Global anchors nevertheless offer broader applicability because they can compare embeddings with different numbers of dimensions. The abstract also identifies advantages for implementation and parallelization, making the equivalent detection capability available through a more flexible comparison method.

The method reveals fine structure in language evolution and domain adaptation. Combined with a graph Laplacian technique, it recovers evolutionary trajectories and domain clusters among disparate corpora. These findings show how pairwise linguistic comparisons can support a broader picture of relationships across collections. The claimed advantage over alignment concerns applicability and computation, alongside equivalent shift-detection ability.
neurips-2018-the-global-anchor-method-fo.tldr: Global anchors detect corpus-level language shifts as effectively as alignment while accommodating embeddings of different dimensionalities.

paragraphs: Video recognition must combine information across time as well as within individual frames. Separating spatial and temporal convolutions is an efficient approach, but ordinary temporal convolution assumes that features at matching image locations are aligned. For moving or deforming content, the same location can refer to different visual content at different times.

The paper introduces TrajectoryNet, which replaces the existing temporal convolution with trajectory convolution. This operation aggregates features along motion paths, explicitly accounting for changes caused by movement or deformation. Its purpose is to combine temporally related content even when that content shifts position across frames, making the aggregation better suited to action recognition.

Experiments on Something-Something and Kinetics show notable improvements over strong baselines. The results support the paper's premise that how temporal features are matched matters, particularly when motion provides crucial evidence about an action. The architectural contribution is a different rule for gathering information across frames: the temporal combination follows trajectories instead of relying on alignment at fixed spatial positions.
neurips-2018-trajectory-convolution-for-.tldr: TrajectoryNet improves action recognition by combining video features along motion paths rather than fixed image locations.

paragraphs: The paper studies how weight normalization controls the capacity of deep networks with rectified linear units. Capacity describes the richness of the functions a model family can represent and matters for analyzing generalization. The authors develop a framework based on Lp,q weight norms and bound the family's Rademacher complexity.

For normalization choices satisfying q ≤ p*, where 1/p + 1/p* = 1, they discuss capacity control that does not depend on network width. Its dependence on depth enters only through a square-root term. The condition on the norm parameters is central: the abstract does not claim this architectural dependence for arbitrary normalization choices.

The analysis also examines approximation, asking how well these normalized networks can represent target functions. For L1,infinity normalization, approximation error can be controlled through the output layer's L1 norm, while the corresponding generalization error depends on architecture only through the square root of depth. Together, these results connect weight-based restrictions to both representational accuracy and generalization, showing how architectural size can enter the guarantees in a limited way.
neurips-2018-understanding-weight-normal.tldr: For specified weight normalizations, ReLU network capacity bounds can avoid width dependence and depend on depth only through its square root.
